Forms

Every text-entry control, with the hint, counter, adornment and validation patterns that go around them. All of them are filled and borderless, and all of them answer focus with a step up the fill ladder rather than with a ring.

Text fields

A field is a block of fill with no border in any state; focus moves it one step brighter rather than drawing a ring around it. Every field pairs a label with its control through for and id.

We only use this to send receipts.

Appears in search results.

Filled variant

Every field is filled in this language, so the modifier has nothing left to add and renders identically to the base. It stays in the contract because a replacement language may well want the distinction back.

Floating label

The label no longer rises out of the box; it sits above it, like every other field label. Floating it means an empty form is a column of boxes whose names vanish the moment anyone starts typing, and a half-filled form shows two label positions at once.

Adornments

Leading and trailing content shares the field's border, so the whole group lights up on focus.

Rich text

A .toolbar over a contenteditable surface. Reach for it only when the formatting is part of the content — a comment box, an article body. For a message or a description, a .textarea is the better control: it is a real form field, it is understood by every assistive technology without help, and it cannot produce markup nobody asked for.

What the toolbar actually does

Select any of this text and press a button. The state of each toggle is read back from the selection, so the strip always describes what is under the caret.

  • Lists, headings and quotations are block commands.
  • Bold, italic and underline are inline, and have the usual shortcuts.
0 words Paste arrives as plain text

This strip wraps to a second row rather than collapsing into an overflow menu, which is the right trade for a formatting toolbar: every command stays visible and in the same place. The two behaviors are alternatives — a wrapping toolbar never overflows, so .toolbar-wrap and data-toolbar-overflowable are not used together.

Two things are worth knowing before shipping this. The formatting goes through document.execCommand, which has been deprecated for years and is still the only way to apply a command to a selection without shipping a text engine — nothing replaced it. And paste is taken as plain text: pasted HTML carries whatever the source page had, including styles, classes and event attributes, and sanitising it needs a parser and an allow-list that this kit does not ship.

The value is mirrored into a hidden textarea marked data-editor-output, so the surrounding form submits it like any other field.

Password strength

Four coarse segments and a word, never a percentage. Nothing computed from the characters alone can tell a strong password from one sitting in a breach list, and a precise-looking score claims an accuracy the estimate does not have.

lock
  • radio_button_unchecked At least 12 characters
  • radio_button_unchecked 16 or more is better still
  • radio_button_unchecked Three of: lower, upper, number, symbol
  • radio_button_unchecked Not one character or pattern repeated
  • radio_button_unchecked Not a commonly used password

Why the rules are listed

A bar on its own only grades. The list is the part that helps someone choose a better password, and it is what the field points at with aria-describedby — the bar itself is aria-hidden, since its meaning is already in the word beside it.

The rules are deliberately weighted towards length. Four character classes in eight characters is a worse password than six plain words, and a composition rule that demands symbols mostly produces one symbol on the end.

Search

A filled box with room for a leading glyph, answering focus the way every other field does. Not a pill: the capsule is kept for the switch track and the scrollbar thumb, and a pill-shaped search bar beside 6px-cornered controls makes a toolbar look assembled from two kits.

Input types

The right type gets the right keyboard on touch devices and free validation in every browser.

Six of these types come with a picker as well as a keyboard — a spinner, a calendar, a clock, a color dialog — and the picker is the one surface on a page that no token can reach. It is drawn by the browser, in the browser’s colors, at the browser’s sizes, with the browser’s radii. In a language built on one set of fills that is not a small inconsistency: an operating-system color dialog opening out of a dark page is not a quieter version of this kit, it is a different program.

So the kit draws its own, and that is the default. Add data-picker to a native input and the shared script replaces the browser’s picker with the component further down this page — the stepper, the calendar, the clock, the month grid, the color panel — keeping the input’s id, its label, its name and its value. Write data-picker="native" to keep the browser’s instead. That is a real choice rather than a concession: the native date field is the one that gets the platform’s own keyboard on a phone, the one that is already localized, and the one people have muscle memory for. It is set per input, so one form can use the kit’s calendar for the field it shows off and the system’s for the field buried in an admin screen. With the script off, every one of these is still a plain semantic input and the browser’s picker is still there.

Formatted inputs

Fields that reshape what is typed: a card number into groups of four, an amount with thousands separators. The mask is presentation and nothing more — it never validates. Whether a card number is real is a question for a checksum and a payment processor, not for a regular expression.

credit_card

Grouping follows the brand: four-four-four-four, or four-six-five for Amex.

North American grouping, as an example — see the warning below.

$

Type into the middle of a value and the caret stays where it was. That is the whole difficulty with a mask: reformatting replaces the value, and the naive version sends the caret to the end, which makes correcting a digit in the middle impossible. The script counts the digits before the caret, rebuilds the value, then puts the caret back after the same number of digits.

warning
Do not mask an international phone number There is no format that fits every country, and forcing one makes valid numbers impossible to enter. A field that has to accept numbers from anywhere should take type="tel", an autocomplete hint and nothing else. The same caution applies to postcodes, names and addresses.

File upload

A drop target wrapping a hidden native input, so dragging, clicking and the keyboard all work. Below it, the same trade for a plain field: the kit supplies the button, the browser supplies the dialog.

Our button, the system’s dialog. The real input is still underneath it — still focusable, still what Tab reaches, still what opens the dialog — so the keyboard path is the browser’s own rather than a reimplementation of it.

Validation

Error state is driven by aria-invalid, which both styles the field and announces it. The message is linked with aria-describedby so it is read out with the field.
